summary: Gives an overview of security considerations when moving from IPv4 to coexisting IPv4 and IPv6 networks, grouped into issues from the IPv6 protocol, from transition mechanisms, and from deployment. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Switching to a new address system while still using the old one makes new ways for trouble to sneak in. This note lists them.

questions: what are ipv6 transition security issues
why are ipv6 routing headers dangerous
subtitle: A tour of the security issues that arise when IPv6 is added alongside IPv4, from the protocol, from transition tricks and from deployment.

tldr.problem: Networks will run IPv4 and IPv6 in parallel for years, and that combination brings new security problems that operators and implementers need to know about.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC groups the issues into three categories: those due to the IPv6 protocol itself, those due to transition mechanisms such as tunnels and relays, and those due to deployment, and suggests mitigations for each.
tldr.outcome: It is an overview, not a standard. It gives administrators a checklist of risks, such as routing headers, fragments, tunnels and ICMPv6 filtering, and argues that secure IPv6 deployment is achievable with careful design.

today: RFC 4942 is an Informational overview. According to the unit metadata it has not been obsoleted or updated, but its advice reflects the state of IPv6 equipment and specifications in 2007.

sections.title: Why Coexistence Matters
sections.content:
The RFC expects IPv6 to be added to IPv4 networks rather than replace them in the short term. It estimates that it will take two or three capital equipment replacement cycles, between nine and 15 years, for IPv6 capabilities to spread, so dual-stack and transition security issues are an ongoing concern.

It also says it describes two matters wrongly identified as IPv6 security concerns in the past: probing and mapping of IPv6 addresses (Appendix A) and privacy (Appendix B).

The RFC warns that some of its filtering rules may drop a small amount of legitimate but unusual traffic, so administrators should log dropped packets and review the logs.
sections.eli5: For a long time, towns will have both old roads and new roads. Each kind of road has its own ways for trouble to creep in, so both need watching.

sections.title: Issues in the IPv6 Protocol Itself
sections.content:
Several features of the base protocol can be abused. Routing headers can evade access controls based on destination address, and a Type 0 header with a spoofed source can help mount reflection attacks. Devices should check both the destination address and any remaining waypoints, and the RFC suggests that Type 0 processing be limited in hosts and some routers.

ICMPv6, unlike ICMP for IPv4, can send error replies to multicast packets, which can amplify denial-of-service attacks. Site-scope multicast addresses such as FF05::2 can reveal key resources, and bogus ICMPv6 errors can disrupt higher-layer protocols. Privacy addresses change often, which can look like DDoS behavior and complicate dynamic DNS updates and address-based policy.

Fragments also matter. Overlapping fragments are a major risk and the RFC says firewalls should drop them. It suggests considering dropping non-final fragments smaller than 640 octets, half the guaranteed minimum MTU of 1280 octets.
sections.eli5: IPv6 has some clever extra features, like letting a letter say which stops to visit on the way. A sneaky sender can misuse those, so guards have to check them.

sections.title: Extension Headers and Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
IPv6 extension headers make firewalls harder to build. To find the transport header, a middlebox must walk the header chain, yet the base specification does not require every header to share a type-length-value layout, and appears to forbid intermediate nodes from processing most headers. The RFC says dropping unknown options may block a useful new extension, while admitting them is a risk, so firewalls should offer a configurable discard policy. It also flags excessive hop-by-hop options, misuse of padding as a covert channel, and overuse of the router alert option.

Neighbor Discovery has its own weakness. Link-local addresses let an attacker start talking on a link with no setup, and Router Advertisements are not integrity protected, so any node can claim to be a router. SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) is the optional mitigation, especially on wireless links. The RFC also notes that IPv4-mapped addresses (::ffff/96) on the wire can be used to bypass access controls.
sections.eli5: Packets can have extra labels stuck on, and a guard has to read them all. A trickster might stick on a lot of strange labels, or pretend to be the traffic officer, so guards need a firm rulebook.

sections.title: Transparency, NATs and Tunnels
sections.content:
IPv6 restores end-to-end addressability that NATs removed in IPv4. The RFC stresses that IPv6 does not require end-to-end connectivity; firewalls can and should still control it. It argues that enterprises should move toward a model with more end-host security and less reliance on the perimeter, and that NAT-PT should be avoided as a general transition mechanism.

Tunnels bring their own dangers: they can make it easier to avoid ingress filtering, expose security mechanisms that depend on a Hop Limit of 255 to attacks from far away, and, for automatic tunnels such as 6to4 and Teredo, require decapsulating traffic from any source. Relays are hard to authenticate. UDP-based tunneling can punch holes in NATs and firewalls, so the RFC says NAT traversal should not be on by default without a similar firewall policy. Tunneled traffic should pass through an IPv4 firewall before decapsulation and then an IPv6 firewall.
sections.eli5: A tunnel is a secret passage under the castle wall. It is handy, but guards need to watch both ends, or someone can sneak in through it.

sections.title: Deployment Pitfalls
sections.content:
The RFC warns against insecure IPv6 pilots: if hosts and routers are not firewalled while the IPv4 service is, the pilot can look bad and delay real deployment. This matters most when IPv6 is on by default in new equipment.

Other deployment points include using small integers as interface identifiers (which makes scanning easy), the many addresses a host may have (which makes access control lists harder to maintain), and ICMPv6, which cannot be dropped wholesale as ICMP sometimes is for IPv4. The RFC also covers IPsec encrypted traffic that perimeter firewalls cannot inspect, resource-limited devices, insecure defaults such as IPv6 telnet being open when only IPv4 telnet was restricted, and proxying of Neighbor Discovery.
sections.eli5: When you open a new door in your house, remember to put a lock on it too. Forgetting is easy because the old doors were already locked.
